summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a history of HCV and alcohol-related cirrhosis, previously treated for hepatocellular carcinoma with TACE, was admitted for severe right upper quadrant and epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting lasting three days. Initial evaluation showed stable cirrhosis without encephalopathy or ascites, and labs revealed pancytopenia consistent with her baseline. Imaging, including a CT scan, did not reveal an acute abdominal cause for her symptoms, but identified a new 14 mm lesion in the liver with arterial enhancement and washout, concerning for recurrent HCC classified as OPTN 5B. Her nausea and pain improved with IV antiemetics and analgesics, and she transitioned to oral intake. She was maintained on her home medications, including lactulose, rifaximin, and spironolactone. The outpatient hepatologist was notified, and follow-up was arranged. She was discharged home with instructions to continue medications, monitor symptoms, obtain outpatient CBC testing, and attend scheduled oncology follow-up for further management of the liver lesion.
